  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Vignette:
# Clinical Vignette: Thea

Thea was twenty-four when she first called for an appointment, her voice steady but clipped on the phone. She worked as an urban planner for the City Department of Transportation, a job she had pursued deliberately—something about designing spaces, mapping safety, controlling the built environment had drawn her. But over the past six months, she had begun to struggle in ways that made even the small office she shared with two colleagues feel increasingly unsafe.

The trauma itself lay in her childhood, though the details remained fragmented in her own mind. She had grown up in a household where her stepfather's discipline had crossed into brutality. The beatings had been unpredictable; she remembered the sound of a belt buckle, the sensation of being cornered in the narrow hallway of their apartment, but when she tried to piece together the timeline or specific incidents, the memories seemed to dissolve. What remained vivid and uncontrollable was the rage. When something triggered a flash of recall—a particular angle of shadow, someone else's raised voice—she would feel a fury so intense it frightened her, as if the rage belonged to someone else entirely and she was merely its vessel. Other times, she would be seized by the full emotional weight of that terror without any accompanying image, just the body memory of being small and trapped and utterly powerless.

Thea had come to believe that what had happened to her was not merely painful but fundamentally unjust. No one in her family had ever acknowledged it directly. Her mother had left when Thea was sixteen; her stepfather had simply disappeared from her life shortly after. There had been no reckoning, no accountability, no moment where the world had recognized what she had endured. This absence of justice had calcified into a kind of permanent wound, one she carried alongside the conviction that she herself was weak—that a stronger person would have found a way to stop it, to escape it, to matter enough to be protected.

She lived alone in a studio apartment in the Capitol Hill neighborhood, and it was the only place she truly felt safe. Anywhere else—her office, the grocery store, friends' homes—carried a low-grade threat that her body registered constantly. At work, she had developed a habit of positioning herself with her back to a wall during meetings, and she flinched visibly whenever a colleague moved suddenly toward her desk. Her supervisor had begun to notice her distraction, the way her concentration would fragment mid-sentence. She had also become someone who agreed to everything. If a coworker asked her to take on an extra project, she said yes. If friends suggested plans, she complied, even when she wanted to refuse. The calculus was simple in her mind: compliance meant she was not a threat, compliance meant she could not be hurt.

The real crisis had come two months ago when her primary care physician had recommended a gynecological ultrasound. Thea had made the appointment, cancelled it, made it again. The thought of lying on an examination table, of being in a position of such physical vulnerability with a stranger's hands near her body, had triggered a cascade of panic. When she finally forced herself to go, she had become so nauseous during the procedure that she had asked the technician to stop. The shame afterward had been immense. She had failed at something a normal person could do without question. It had reinforced her deepest belief: she was weak, fundamentally fragile in a way that others were not.

What brought her to therapy was not a single incident but an accumulation. She had begun to spend entire evenings imagining alternative lives—versions of herself where her stepfather had never existed in her home, where she had grown up in a different house, a different family. These counterfactual spirals would consume hours, leaving her exhausted and no closer to the life she actually inhabited. She had also noticed that being seen—truly seen by others—had become intolerable. In the office, she wore large sweaters and kept her head down. When friends commented on her appearance or asked how she was really doing, she felt a sharp discomfort, as if being observed was itself a form of violation. She had come to believe that if people truly knew her, truly understood what had happened to her and how it had broken something inside, they would see her not as a person but as an object of pity, or worse, as someone who deserved what had happened.

Now, sitting in the therapist's office, Thea was hoping that someone could help her understand why the past refused to stay in the past, and whether the person she had become—careful, compliant, trapped in a shrinking world—was all that remained.
